turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was a section with numbers, prices I think, and it took me longer than I expected to find the main one. Something about the way the numbers were presented didn't quite add up for me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the numbers were presented didn't quite add up for me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy in the Order Summary, specifically how the price for the Wireless Mouse ($39.99) is displayed in a much larger font than the other prices, making it look like the total cost rather than an individual item price.
B) The mathematical inconsistency where the Subtotal ($288.99) and Total ($288.99) match exactly, despite the listed items adding up to $289.00 (since $249 + $39.99 = $288.99 is mathematically incorrect).
C) The layout of the final cost breakdown at the bottom of the summary box, where "Subtotal," "Shipping," and "Total" are stacked vertically without clear visual separation or alignment to the right column.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? The sizes not forming a clear hierarchy, or not being able to spot the total without reading through everything. I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it.

turns.q: What specific visual cues in that line item make it stand out more than the other prices?
turns.a: I suppose... looking at the price section, I wasn't quite sure which number was the most important one. There were several different sizes of text in that section and I couldn't immediately read the hierarchy from them. Not a dramatic problem — I did find the total after reading through — but it took longer than it should have, I think.

turns.q: What specific visual differences between that price and the others make it difficult for you to distinguish which number is the total?
turns.a: I suppose it was the sizing. There were several different text sizes in that section — some larger, some smaller — but not arranged in any pattern I could follow. So my eye didn't know where to go first. I'm not sure if that was intentional — maybe they wanted to show different levels of detail — but it meant I couldn't scan the section the way I'd normally scan prices.

turns.q: What specifically about that lack of a consistent pattern makes it difficult for you to determine which price is the most important one?
turns.a: I'm not entirely sure. Maybe because the numbers were all different sizes but not in a way that felt intentional. I've seen other apps where the total is obviously the main number — you can see it without reading. Here I couldn't do that. I had to read the labels. I don't know if that's a problem or just how this particular layout works.

turns.q: What would those price labels need to look like for you to immediately know which one is the total without reading the text?
turns.a: I keep coming back to the same answer — the sizes didn't feel organized in a readable way. I'm not sure I can explain it beyond that. It's one of those things that's easier to feel than to articulate.

turns.q: What specific changes to the text sizes would make the price hierarchy feel organized and readable to you?
turns.a: I think I've said most of what I have to say about it. I keep coming back to the same point because that's where the concern actually is — it's not something more complex underneath. At least not from where I'm standing. It's genuinely just about which number I can spot immediately and which ones I have to hunt for.

turns.q: What specific adjustments to the text sizes would make the total cost immediately obvious without requiring you to hunt for it?
turns.a: I keep coming back to the same answer — the sizes didn't feel organized in a readable way. I'm not sure I can explain it beyond that. It's one of those things that's easier to feel than to articulate.

turns.q: Would making the total price bold and larger than all individual item prices help you spot it immediately, or is the issue that the labels (like "Total" vs "Subtotal") aren't distinct enough from the numbers themselves?
turns.a: I don't think I can put it any more precisely than that. The text varied in size but not in a way that helped me. I'm not sure there's a clearer way for me to describe why.

turns.q: What specific changes to the text sizes would make the total cost immediately obvious without requiring you to hunt for it?
turns.a: I'm aware I keep saying the same thing, but it really does come down to that — there were too many different sizes and none of them clearly meant "this is the most important." I don't have a sharper way to phrase it.

turns.q: If you were adjusting those text sizes to make the total stand out clearly, what specific change would you make to ensure it looks more important than the individual item prices?
turns.a: I guess if I think about it, it's probably the sizing — there were so many different text sizes in that section that none of them felt dominant. Size usually signals importance, I'd think, but it wasn't doing that here. Nothing was clearly the main number.

turns.q: Would having just two distinct text sizes—one large for the total and one small for everything else—solve this, or do you think the issue is that the "Total" label itself isn't visually distinct enough from the item names?
turns.a: I guess if I think about it, it's probably the sizing — there were so many different text sizes in that section that none of them felt dominant. Size usually signals importance, I'd think, but it wasn't doing that here. Nothing was clearly the main number.
